rv.q: Mark Rylance is once again ruling audiences at the Belasco Theater, where the strangely enchanting “Farinelli and the King,” Claire van Kampen’s shimmering fairy tale for grown-ups, opened on Sunday night.
Watching Rylance convey the pain, fear and vulnerability of that striving is heart-rending and unforgettable.
Like you do if you are Rylance, who dives deep inside wacky Philippe in a performance as empathetic as it is seemingly spontaneous.
But mad kings could easily become a specialty with this actor, who sees the pathos and the ridiculousness of the royal personage, and warmly embraces them both.
The result is a show that is all frosting and no cake.

Unlike in Alan Bennett’s play The Madness of George III, and its film adaptation, the deteriorating mental health of a monarch here doesn’t constitute a sustaining narrative arc, even if Rylance’s commanding performance remains the center of attention.
The pleasures of John Dove's production—the music, Rylance's halting propulsion, Jonathan Fensom's sumptuous sets and costumes—gleam to no purpose, real jewels glued to a trinket crown.
The characters feel largely static — beautifully sung by Davies and powerfully acted by Rylance, but not very dynamic.
Meticulously off-handed, it’s funny and sad, a performance to be savored in a totally engaging little triumph of a show.
While it would be satisfying enough to simply embrace Rylance's mastery and the glorious works of (mostly) Handel, there is a more significant message.
This is plenty enough to put Farinelli and the King on the highly recommended list.

It may contain arias from obscure Baroque operas and candlelit chandeliers, but the play is, at heart, a straightforward and sentimental “bromance,” one in which Farinelli is willing to give up adoring audiences all over Europe to serve at the king’s command.
English playwright Claire van Kampen’s fact-based but liberally embroidered drama isn’t so sensational — and can't get past one obstacle.
Whatever, your eyes and ears will leave Farinelli happy indeed.
Van Kampen’s disjointed storytelling and John Dove’s pedestrian direction, however, turn it into something nearer soap opera — but without either the intrigue or the sex of that lesser genre.
It's nevertheless an enjoyable venture, with the sumptuousness of director John Dove's production helping to mask the flaws.
After the king exits for good, only the superb music can keep the audience awake.

But for the performance of Rylance, who is as always remarkable, and Davies, who is a delicious surprise and deserving of the two final bows that Rylance engineers, Farinelli and The King remains a tedious bit of business.
